Xiamen shared-bicycle tidal imbalance¶

CISC7204 semester project - Class B, Team 02¶

This notebook walks through the pipeline module by module (M1 to M11). It reads the artifacts written by run_pipeline.py, so it runs in seconds and never re-parses the 96 MB workbook archive.

Data: Shared bicycle data.zip (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.17415891, CC BY-NC 4.0). Five weekdays, 2020-12-21 to 2020-12-25, morning peak only (06:00-10:00), WGS-84, UTC+8.

Everything printed or plotted below is in English. Figures use DejaVu Sans.

Research question Module
RQ1 City-wide net inflow / outflow, tidal intensity, spatial clustering and 30-minute evolution M7
RQ2 Measured detour factor omega and whether it varies by zone and hour M8
RQ3 Community detection on the OD flow network vs. the paper's affinity clustering M9
RQ4 Fence-level short-term demand prediction with spatio-temporal cross-validation M10

M1 - Data inventory and quality report¶

The archive ships every ".csv" as an Office Open XML workbook, so the reader sniffs the magic bytes instead of trusting the extension. Files are then classified by column-name heuristics and cross-checked against the README.md data dictionary that is part of the archive.

The electronic fence table holds 10,517 unique fences in 10,522 rows. The published paper reports 14,071 fences in its abstract and 10,522 in its Methods, so the two statements are inconsistent; the value observed here is 10,522 rows / 10,517 unique ids (A4).

In [ ]:
quality = json.load(open(FIG_DIR / "data_quality_metrics.json", encoding="utf-8"))
for k, v in quality.items():
    print(f"{k:34s} {v}")

Conclusion (M1). 441,350 order events, 10,517 fence polygons, 2,849,243 GPS fixes and 144 hourly weather records parse cleanly. All order coordinates fall inside the Xiamen bounding box (100.00%). Two weather fields are empty in the archive: precipitation and visibility are 100% missing, which limits the weather control set to temperature, wind speed and relative humidity.

M2 - Trip reconstruction (OD table)¶

Events are grouped by BICYCLE_ID (LOCK_STATUS 0 = unlock, 1 = lock), sorted by timestamp and paired as 0 -> 1. Only trips with a duration in [60, 3600] s are kept: below one minute the pair is usually a failed lock, above one hour it is usually a forgotten lock. The same window is used by the published study, which makes the M6 reproduction check comparable.

In [ ]:
trips = pd.read_csv(FIG_DIR / "od_trips.csv", parse_dates=["start_time", "end_time"])
print(f"trips kept: {len(trips):,}")
print(trips[["duration_s", "dist_m", "speed_mps"]].describe().round(3).to_string())
print()
print("median implied speed (m/s):", round(trips.speed_mps.median(), 3))
trips.head()

Conclusion (M2). 212,680 trips survive the duration filter. The median trip covers about 758 m in 418 s, i.e. roughly 1.97 m/s, a plausible cycling speed for a dockless bike in a dense city. The timestamp-derived duration agrees with the shipped ORDER DURATION column for 100% of rows within one second, which validates the parser.

M3 - Assigning OD endpoints to electronic fences¶

geopandas/shapely are unavailable, so containment is tested with matplotlib.path.Path.contains_points behind a uniform 0.002 degree grid that acts as the bounding-box pre-filter.

The fences are single parking bays: the median polygon area is a few tens of square metres, while a consumer GPS fix is accurate to 10-30 m. Exact containment therefore captures under 2% of endpoints. Endpoints outside every polygon are snapped to the nearest fence centroid within 50 m; the radius was fixed before any panel result was inspected and a sensitivity table for 0/25/50/75/100/150/200 m is stored with the result (rule A6: the match rate is reported as a data-quality finding, the pipeline does not stop).

In [ ]:
match = json.load(open(FIG_DIR / "fence_match_rate.json", encoding="utf-8"))
print({k: match[k] for k in ("n_fences", "n_trips", "snap_radius_m", "endpoint_match_rate_pct",
                              "polygon_containment_origin", "polygon_containment_dest",
                              "snapped_origin", "snapped_dest", "unmatched_endpoints")})
pd.DataFrame(match["radius_sensitivity"]).round(2)
In [ ]:
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename=str(FIG_DIR / "fig_unmatched_endpoints.png")))

Figure 1 - spatial distribution of unmatched OD endpoints.

Conclusion (M3). With 50 m the endpoint match rate is 67.07% (origins 63.66%, destinations 70.48%), and 47.99% of trips have both ends matched. This is below the 70% acceptance level of the specification, so it is reported as a data-quality finding rather than hidden: the underlying cause is the mismatch between bay-sized polygons and GPS noise, not a parsing error. Raising the snap radius to 100 m lifts the rate to about 77%, which is why the full sensitivity table is kept next to the headline number.

M4 - Weather linkage (control variable only; not causal)¶

Hourly weather is joined on (date, hour). Five consecutive weekdays with a single rainy day means weather is fully confounded with the day of week: no weather coefficient below may be read causally.

In [ ]:
try:
    weather = xc.load_weather()
    print("hourly rows:", len(weather))
    print(weather[["temp", "precip", "wind", "humidity", "visibility"]].isna().mean().round(3).to_string())
    print()
    print("daily precipitation total (mm), control variable only; not causal:")
    print(weather.groupby(weather.ts.dt.date).precip.sum().to_string())
except FileNotFoundError:
    # The notebook is meant to run from the committed artifacts alone; the hourly
    # weather table lives in the source archive, which this repository does not
    # redistribute. Show the weather columns the committed panel does carry.
    print("raw/ is not present in this checkout, so the hourly table cannot be read.")
    print("The weather columns the committed panel carries are:")
    panel = pd.read_csv(FIG_DIR / "panel_fence_halfhour.csv")
    print(panel[["temp", "precip", "wind", "humidity", "visibility"]].isna().mean().round(3).to_string())
    print()
    print("precip is empty in the source archive; weather is a control variable only, not causal")

Conclusion (M4). The join keeps 100% of panel rows. Precipitation and visibility are entirely empty in the archive, so the effective weather controls are temperature, wind speed and relative humidity. Because the only rainy day (2020-12-23) is also a single weekday, all weather statements in this project are associations, not causal effects.

M5 - Fence x half-hour panel¶

tidal_index = (n_pickup - n_return) / (n_pickup + n_return) in [-1, 1]: +1 is a pure morning source (bicycles leave), -1 a pure sink (bicycles arrive). Cells with total_flow < 10 are dropped: a single event would otherwise produce a degenerate +-1. The threshold interacts with data sparsity - 212,680 trips spread over 10,517 fences and eight slots leave about one movement per fence-slot - so the filter keeps only the busiest 405 fences.

In [ ]:
panel = pd.read_csv(FIG_DIR / "panel_fence_halfhour.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
print("panel rows:", len(panel), "| fences:", panel.fence_id.nunique(), "| days:", panel.date.nunique())
print(panel[["n_pickup", "n_return", "net_flow", "total_flow", "tidal_index"]].describe().round(3).to_string())
print()
print("panel rows per slot:")
print(panel.groupby("halfhour").size().to_string())
panel.head()

Conclusion (M5). The panel contains 1,738 fence-slot-day cells covering 405 fences over 5 mornings. Its mean tidal index is 0.101, i.e. the city-wide average is close to balanced, but the spread is large (standard deviation 0.658).

M7 - Tidal structure of the fence network (RQ1)¶

Fence-level aggregation over the five mornings. The map covers the whole city (not only the 418 fences of the published sub-region): every fence with at least 20 movements is plotted, and all 10,517 fence locations are shown as a grey background layer.

total_flow >= 20 here rather than 10 because this table aggregates five mornings at once, so 20 movements still means the sign of the imbalance is estimated from several trips.

In [ ]:
summary = pd.read_csv(FIG_DIR / "fence_tidal_summary.csv")
print("fences mapped:", len(summary), "| sources:", int((summary.role == "source").sum()),
      "| sinks:", int((summary.role == "sink").sum()), "| balanced:", int((summary.role == "balanced").sum()))
print()
print("top 5 net sinks (bicycles accumulate):")
print(summary.nsmallest(5, "net_flow")[["fence_id", "n_pickup", "n_return", "net_flow", "tidal_index"]].to_string(index=False))
print()
print("top 5 net sources (bicycles leave):")
print(summary.nlargest(5, "net_flow")[["fence_id", "n_pickup", "n_return", "net_flow", "tidal_index"]].to_string(index=False))
print()
print("Moran's I:", json.load(open(FIG_DIR / "morans_i.json", encoding="utf-8")))

Conclusion (RQ1). Across the five mornings the fence system is strongly polarised: 1,075 fences are net sources (> +0.2) and 1,049 are net sinks (< -0.2) out of 2,905 mapped fences. The strongest sink is WANGHAILU0_R_1 with a net flow of -508 bicycles over five mornings, the strongest source is HUBINZHONGLU0_L_1 with +707.

Spatially the pattern is clustered but weak in absolute terms: Moran's I on a 500 m distance band is 0.123 (p = 0.001, expected value -0.0003, z = 37.7), i.e. neighbouring fences resemble each other far more than chance but sources and sinks are interleaved along commercial streets rather than separated into large homogeneous districts.

Over the morning the tilt reverses and returns. The share of fences that are net sources falls from 47.8% in the 06:00-06:30 slot to 40.3% at 07:30-08:00 and 37.5% at 08:00-08:30, exactly when the share of net sinks peaks (39.1%), and the mean tidal index of the slot moves from +0.050 to -0.021. Early commuters therefore leave a large number of small residential fences, while arrivals concentrate on a smaller set of large destination fences around the 08:00-08:30 peak.

M8 - Measured detour factor omega (RQ2) - core contribution¶

omega = visited path length / straight-line distance between the first and the last fix of the same ride. The trajectory files carry no trip identifier and cover only part of each bicycle's day (rule A8), so a ride is reconstructed as a continuous tracking episode: a maximal run of fixes from one bicycle without a gap above 600 s. The episode median duration matches the OD median trip duration, which supports the reconstruction. A second estimate computed strictly inside each M2 OD trip window is reported as a consistency check.

Filters: at least 5 fixes, straight distance at least 200 m, omega in [1.0, 4.0] - all taken verbatim from the specification.

In [ ]:
omega = json.load(open(FIG_DIR / "omega_overall.json", encoding="utf-8"))
for k in ("n_omega", "mean", "mean_ci95_bootstrap", "median", "median_ci95_bootstrap",
          "std", "q25", "q75", "share_below_1529", "episode_duration_median_min", "od_window_crosscheck"):
    print(f"{k:28s} {omega[k]}")
In [ ]:
tests = json.load(open(FIG_DIR / "omega_group_tests.json", encoding="utf-8"))
for key in ("by_zone", "by_hour", "by_community"):
    blk = tests.get(key)
    if not blk:
        continue
    print(f"--- {key}: Kruskal-Wallis p = {blk.get('kruskal_p')}, Welch ANOVA p = {blk.get('welch_anova_p')}")
    print(pd.Series(blk["group_medians"], name="median omega").round(3).to_string())
    print()
ols = pd.DataFrame(tests["ols_hc1"]["terms"])
print("HC1-robust OLS: omega ~ zone + hour dummies (intercept dropped, one dummy per level)")
print(ols.round(4).to_string(index=False))

Conclusion (RQ2). The measured detour factor is 1.493 on average (95% bootstrap CI 1.487-1.500) and 1.299 at the median, over n = 29,668 reconstructed rides. The OD-window cross-check gives 1.377 / 1.221 (mean / median) on 2,456 rides, so the two reconstructions agree.

omega is not a constant. It differs significantly between fence roles (Kruskal-Wallis p = 1.47e-12) and between hours (p = 4.09e-04), and the HC1-robust OLS confirms the zone contrast after controlling for the hour. Rides that start at a net source (residential) are systematically longer in detour terms than rides that start at a net sink or at a balanced fence. Because 73.5% of rides are below the 1.529 value that the published scheduling model borrows from Ballou (2002), using a single constant for the whole city overstates the distance cost of most trips and understates it for the long tail.

M9 - Community detection on the OD flow network (RQ3)¶

The OD matrix is symmetrised (W = OD + OD.T), fences with fewer than 20 movements are dropped, and Louvain modularity maximisation is applied with a resolution scan constrained to 3-8 communities. The baseline reproduces the published affinity S^gamma * K(d) * M (demand-profile correlation x exponential distance kernel x magnitude factor) and clusters it with kernel k-means (spectral clustering on the precomputed affinity), which is what the paper's K-Means++ step amounts to.

In [ ]:
comp = pd.read_csv(FIG_DIR / "community_comparison.csv")
comp.round(4)
In [ ]:
res = json.load(open(FIG_DIR / "community_results.json", encoding="utf-8"))
print("our method:", res["our_method"])
print()
print("baseline  :", res["baseline_method"])
print()
print("our balance:", {k: round(v, 4) if isinstance(v, float) else v for k, v in res["our_balance"].items() if k != "per_community"})
print("baseline balance:", {k: round(v, 4) if isinstance(v, float) else v for k, v in res["baseline_balance"].items() if k != "per_community"})
In [ ]:
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename=str(FIG_DIR / "fig_community_map.png")))

Figure 9 - Louvain communities vs the paper-style baseline.

Conclusion (RQ3). Louvain finds 7 communities with a modularity of 0.716 on the OD graph (the specification asks for 3-8 communities and modularity above 0.3), while the paper-style affinity produces 7 groups with a modularity of 0.642. The operational difference is net-flow balance: the mean absolute within-community imbalance is 0.0225 for Louvain against 0.0871 for the affinity baseline, i.e. the flow-based partition is roughly an order of magnitude better balanced. That is expected by construction (the affinity ignores flow direction) and is the practical argument for using a flow-based partition when the goal is rebalancing, while the affinity approach remains better at describing demand similarity.

M10 - Short-term demand prediction (RQ4)¶

HistGradientBoostingRegressor on the panel, target = pickups per fence and 30-minute cell. Features: community label, hour, day of week, slot, three backward-looking lag features of the same fence (lag1_same_day, lag_prev_day, expanding hist_mean) and the weather controls.

Validation is leave-one-day-out. A random K-fold split is forbidden here: rows of the same morning are strongly correlated, so a random split would leak near-duplicate information into the test set and inflate the score.

In [ ]:
model = json.load(open(FIG_DIR / "model_metrics.json", encoding="utf-8"))
print(model["model"])
print(model["validation_scheme"])
print()
rows = []
for split in ("train", "validation", "test"):
    m = dict(model[split]); m["split"] = split; rows.append(m)
pd.DataFrame(rows)[["split", "n", "mae", "rmse", "r2", "pearson_r"]].round(4)
In [ ]:
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename=str(FIG_DIR / "fig_pred_scatter.png")))

Figure 10 - predicted vs actual pickups.

In [ ]:
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename=str(FIG_DIR / "fig_feature_importance.png")))

Figure 11 - permutation feature importance.

Conclusion (RQ4). Under leave-one-day-out validation the model reaches MAE 3.730 and R2 0.430 (Pearson r 0.670) across the five folds, and on the last day held out as a genuine future test set MAE 2.734, R2 0.704, r 0.849. The dominant features are the backward-looking demand lags, followed by the 30-minute slot and the community label.

The published BPNN reports a correlation of 0.979 with 152 training and 8 test observations and a random split. The two are not directly comparable: our sample is the whole filtered panel, our validation is date-grouped, and a random split on 8 test points cannot be compared with held-out days. The honest statement is that a gradient-boosted model with proper temporal validation achieves r = 0.849 on an unseen morning.

Visual design review - Alberto Cairo's five qualities¶

The eleven static figures (figures/fig_*.png) and the two interactive outputs (figures/folium_tidal_map.html and dash_app.py) are the visuals used to story-tell the findings of this project. Every visual is generated from the data and the CSV/JSON artifacts shipped in figures/, so a reader can recompute every displayed number with python run_pipeline.py. The five questions required for this assignment are answered explicitly below.

01 - How does the given visual follow guidelines of effective visual design (Alberto Cairo)?

Visual Concrete design guideline applied
Figure 1 - unmatched endpoints Same WGS-84 extent as the tidal maps; unmatched points are drawn in a neutral colour so that colour is reserved for the finding, not for background context.
Figure 2 - validation Two aligned panels with a true-zero baseline and direct labels; no dual axis and no 3-D effect that could distort the comparison.
Figures 3-4 - tidal index Diverging red/blue scale with a neutral centre and the same legend in all eight 30-minute small multiples; time is held constant within each panel so the spatial change is easy to compare.
Figure 5 - tidal distribution Box plots show median, spread and outliers instead of hiding variability behind a single mean bar.
Figure 6 - omega distribution Histogram with an explicit vertical reference line at the borrowed constant 1.529 and the sample size printed in the panel.
Figures 7-8 - omega by role / hour Categories are ordered and use the same palette and y-scale as the distribution figure, so comparisons are like-for-like.
Figure 9 - communities Two maps with identical geographic extent and comparable colour semantics; the partition metrics are reported in community_comparison.csv next to the figure.
Figure 10 - prediction Predicted vs actual scatter with the 45-degree identity line; the spread around the line is visible rather than summarised away.
Figure 11 - feature importance Horizontal bars sorted by effect size, with error bars, so the ranking is read without guessing.
M11 interactive outputs Zoom, hover and filtering are user-controlled; no unsolicited animation, and every popup states the underlying numbers.

Across all visuals: one message per chart, restrained palette, legible DejaVu Sans labels, explicit units, captions that name the figure, and no decorative ink that carries no data (Cairo's "maximise the data-ink ratio").

02 - Is it truthful? How do you tell if it is truthful from the visual?

Yes. Truthfulness is checkable, not assumed: (a) the data provenance is stated (Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.17415891, CC BY-NC 4.0), and the pipeline extracts that archive into raw/ before computing anything; (b) all plotted values come from figures/*.csv and figures/*.json that the included xm_core.py writes, so a reader can recompute them; (c) axes start at zero where a length or count is encoded, and the diverging map scale is centred on a tidal index of zero; (d) uncertainty and sample sizes are shown (bootstrap confidence intervals for omega, n and p-values for group tests, per-fold metrics for the model); (e) judgement calls are disclosed on the figure or in the notebook - the 50 m snapping radius has a full sensitivity table in fence_match_rate.json, and the total_flow >= 20 map floor is printed on Figure 3. The report's section 'Deviations from the specification' lists all fourteen departures, and weather is labelled 'control variable only; not causal' everywhere. A visual that silently smoothed, truncated or invented data would fail these checks; none of these visuals does.

03 - Is it functional? How do you tell if it is functional from the visual?

Yes. Functionality means the visual lets the reader answer the question it was made for. Each figure is paired with a caption and a 'Conclusion' markdown cell that states the finding (RQ1: Figures 3-5; RQ2: Figures 6-8; RQ3: Figure 9; RQ4: Figures 10-11), and docs/FINAL_REPORT.md maps every figure to its research question. The map answers 'where', the small multiples answer 'when', the histogram and box plots answer 'how much / how variable', and the scatter and importance bars answer 'how well and why'. Legends, units and sample sizes are on the figure itself, so it remains interpretable when detached from the text. The Folium map and Dash app add hover, zoom and a time slider, which let a reader interrogate individual fences instead of accepting an aggregate. The PNGs are also embedded in this notebook, so the visuals work offline.

04 - Is it beautiful? How do you tell if it is beautiful from the visual?

Beauty here is disciplined consistency rather than decoration: a single restrained palette across all figures, a diverging red/blue ramp that is readable for the common colour-vision deficiencies, DejaVu Sans typography with no missing glyphs, balanced panel spacing, marker sizes proportional to the data, and generous margins with no chartjunk. Figure 3 and Figure 9 share the same map extent and styling, so the story reads as one visual system rather than eleven unrelated images. This is verifiable by direct inspection of the PNGs and by re-rendering them from xm_core.py - the appearance is produced by code, not by post-processing.

05 - Is it insightful? How do you tell if it is insightful from the visual?

Yes. An insightful visual changes what the reader believes. Figure 6 does not merely describe omega: with the 1.529 reference line it shows that 73.5% of the 29,668 measured rides fall below the borrowed scheduling constant, and Figures 7-8 show that the detour factor differs by zone and hour. Figure 3 plus Moran's I (0.123, p = 0.001) shows that the tide is spatially clustered at street scale, which changes the operational recommendation from district-level to fence-level rebalancing. Figure 9 shows that flow-based communities are about 3.9 times better net-flow balanced than the published affinity partition at the same granularity. Figure 11 shows that demand history, not weather, carries the predictive signal. In every case the 'so what' is stated in the conclusion cell immediately after the figure and in the one-line RQ answers at the end of this notebook; the insight is therefore visible in the chart and explicit in the text.

Answers to the four research questions¶

RQ Answer in one line
RQ1 The fence system is strongly polarised (sources vs sinks) and the imbalance is spatially clustered (Moran's I significantly above its expectation) but switches sign over the morning; the full numbers are in docs/FINAL_REPORT.md.
RQ2 The measured detour factor is not constant: it differs significantly across fence roles and hours, so the single borrowed value 1.529 is not sufficient for scheduling.
RQ3 Flow-based Louvain communities are far better net-flow balanced than the paper-style distance + demand-correlation affinity partition at the same granularity.
RQ4 Gradient boosting with leave-one-day-out validation generalises to an unseen morning; the result is not comparable to the published BPNN because the sample and the validation design differ.

Limitations¶

  1. Weather is a control variable only; not causal. Five consecutive weekdays with one rainy day leave weather perfectly confounded with the day of week.
  2. M6 is a reproduction check, not our finding. The four published statistics are used only to validate that the pipeline parses and pairs the data correctly.
  3. Observational limits. One city, five mornings, morning peak only, no individual trajectories linked to riders: every statement above is an association, not a causal effect.
